parts.title: Triage in the Emergency Department
parts.frequencyBadge: Predicted: Very High · Tested in 4 of 5 past papers
parts.description: Principles, requirements, high-risk groups and triage errors: the most repeated section of the paper.

questions.text: State five (5) principles of triage.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Very High · Triage appeared as an SAQ in 4 of 5 past papers

askedIn.wording: State five (5) principles of triage.

modelAnswer.intro: Triage is the rapid sorting of patients arriving at the emergency department to decide who must be seen immediately and who can safely wait. The principles are the rules that guide how that sorting is done. The lecture notes list six, so learn all six and write the five you can explain best.

subsections.heading: A. Five principles to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. It is not first come, first served: patients are seen according to the urgency of their condition, not the order of arrival.
2. Acuity is assessed and categorised against set criteria (for example CTAS), so decisions are objective and consistent.
3. Set timelines for assessment are based on acuity (for example level 1 immediately, level 2 within 15 minutes).
4. Treatment starts promptly for seriously ill or injured patients, even while they are still in the triage area.
5. Triage is dynamic: a patient's status can change rapidly, so patients are reassessed and re-categorised.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable points
points: 6. Triage relies on multidisciplinary teamwork between the triage nurse, doctors and the rest of the emergency team.
7. The initial triage assessment is brief and should be completed within 5 minutes of arrival.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write each principle as one short, complete statement. The first principle, 'not first come, first served', is the one examiners expect to see.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Triage section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: the question asks for PRINCIPLES (the rules of triage). Do not write the importance of triage (why it is done), the roles of the triage nurse (what she does) or the CTAS levels. Marks are deducted for information not asked for.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Use the four-question frame to avoid mixing up triage questions: WHY (importance), WHAT the nurse does (roles), RULES (principles), WHAT IS NEEDED (requirements).
Memory tip 2: Principle number one is always 'not first come, first served'. Write it first and you secure the easiest mark.
Memory tip 3: Six principles, six letters: SORTED. If you blank in the exam, say SORTED and the points come back.
Memory tip 4: Remember that 'dynamic' means the triage category is not final. This links to the reassessment points in other triage questions.

tips: Marking rule: 1 mark per distinct principle, so write exactly five numbered points. Extra points earn nothing and risk deductions.

questions.text: State four (4) requirements of a triage area.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Very High · Same lecture section as the 4 triage SAQs already tested

askedIn.wording: State four (4) requirements of a triage area.

modelAnswer.intro: A triage area must be set up so that patients can be assessed quickly, privately and safely, and so that the findings can be recorded against the right patient. The notes list six requirements; four are enough for this question.

subsections.heading: A. Four requirements to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. A trained triage health worker (nurse) who can assess and categorise patients using the triage tool.
2. A private room, to maintain patient confidentiality during the interview and examination.
3. A desk with two chairs, or a couch, for the interview and for examining the patient.
4. A monitor for blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation (SpO2) and temperature, to take triage vital signs.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable requirements
points: 5. The patient record chart, to document the chief complaint, findings and triage category.
6. Three patient identifiers: full (three) names, date of birth and hospital registration number, to make sure the right patient is matched to the right record.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Name each requirement and add one short purpose where possible (for example 'private room for confidentiality'). If the examiner asks for five, add the record chart.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Triage section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: 'requirements of a triage area' means what must be available there. Do not write the triage process, the principles or the roles of the nurse.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Picture the triage cubicle and list what you see: a nurse, a room, a desk, a monitor, a chart and a wristband with three IDs.
Memory tip 2: The three identifiers are the full three names, date of birth and registration number. 'Name, Birthday, Number'.
Memory tip 3: The monitor measures the five physiological readings you will also need in other questions: BP, HR, RR, SpO2 and temperature.
Memory tip 4: PRIMED gives you all six requirements in one word.

tips: Marking rule: 1 mark per requirement. Write exactly the number asked (four) and stop.
Keywords the examiner looks for: trained nurse, private room or confidentiality, desk and chairs or couch, monitor (BP, HR, RR, SpO2, temperature), record chart, three identifiers.
Do not confuse requirements (what the area needs) with the equipment for scene safety (collar, backboard, oxygen, trauma bag), which belongs to a different question.

questions.text: State three (3) categories of patients who are considered high risk during triage and give one example for each.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Short lecture list that fits a 3-mark SAQ

askedIn.wording: State three (3) categories of patients who are considered high risk during triage and give one example for each.

modelAnswer.intro: High-risk patients are those who can deteriorate quickly or hide the seriousness of their illness. The triage nurse must be extra cautious with them and should not under-triage them.

subsections.heading: A. Three categories to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Children under 5 years: for example, an infant under 4 weeks old should be seen in under 10 minutes.
2. Adults over 65 years: for example, an elderly patient with a minor-looking complaint who may have a serious hidden illness.
3. Patients with comorbidities: for example, hypertension, diabetes, cardiac or respiratory disease, neurological deficits or sickle cell disease.

subsections.heading: B. Why they need extra caution
points: 4. Under-triage of these groups delays care and risks deterioration, so the triage nurse gives them a higher level of suspicion and reassesses them more often.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write the category and an example on the same line so that the examiner sees both parts of the question.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Triage section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not list CTAS levels or the triage vital signs. The question asks only for the high-risk groups and an example for each.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Remember 5-65-Co: under 5, over 65, and comorbid.
Memory tip 2: Infants under 4 weeks are the 'under 10 minutes' group. It is the one number in this list.
Memory tip 3: The comorbidity examples are the same illnesses you meet in nursing practice every day: HTN, DM, cardiac, respiratory, neuro and sickle cell.

mnemonics.source: Original study aid built from the attached lecture notes

aceItTip.title: Examiner Scoring Key & Common Pitfalls
tips: Marking rule: 1 mark per category with its example. Three lines, three marks.
Keywords the examiner looks for: under 5 years, over 65 years, comorbidities with a named example.
If the question asks 'why' these patients are high risk, add that they deteriorate quickly and are at risk of under-triage.

questions.text: Differentiate between under-triage and over-triage.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · Short 'severity rating' definitions from the triage notes

askedIn.wording: Differentiate between under-triage and over-triage.

modelAnswer.intro: Triage assigns each patient a severity rating. When the rating does not match the patient's true condition, the result is either under-triage or over-triage. Both are errors, but they harm patients and the department in different ways.

subsections.heading: A. Four points to write (2 marks for each term)
points: 1. Under-triage: the patient is given a lower acuity level than the condition really needs (for example, a patient with chest pain and sweating is given a non-urgent category).
2. Consequence of under-triage: care is delayed and the patient risks deterioration.
3. Over-triage: the patient is given a higher acuity level than the condition really needs (for example, a patient with a mild sore throat is sent to the resuscitation area).
4. Consequence of over-triage: it diverts resources (staff, rooms and equipment) from the patients who need them most.

subsections.heading: B. How to reduce both errors
points: 5. Use set criteria, take vital signs, apply extra caution with high-risk patients and reassess whenever the patient's condition changes.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Define each term first, then give its effect. Compare them directly using the words 'lower' and 'higher'.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Triage section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: 'Differentiate' needs both terms and their difference. A definition of triage alone earns no marks.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: UNDER means too low a level: the patient is in danger. OVER means too high a level: the system is overloaded.
Memory tip 2: Think of a scale that is set too low for the patient (under) or too high (over).

tips: Marking rule: a definition and a consequence for each term, so four points for four marks.
Keywords the examiner looks for: lower or higher acuity, delays care, risks deterioration, diverts resources.
Use the word 'whereas' or a two-column layout to show the difference clearly.

questions.partTitle: Trauma Assessment: Primary and Secondary Survey
questions.text: Outline five (5) nursing interventions in the management of the airway of a trauma patient.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Primary survey is tested every year in the MCQs and is ready to cross over to the SAQs

askedIn.wording: Outline five (5) nursing interventions in the management of the airway of a trauma patient.

modelAnswer.intro: In the primary survey the airway comes first, with the cervical spine protected at the same time. The nurse looks for signs of airway trouble, such as secretions, a foreign body, bleeding, facial or neck injury, inability to speak, retractions, reduced consciousness or pale or cyanosed skin, and then acts at once.

subsections.heading: A. Five interventions to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Suction the airway and remove loose objects such as teeth and debris, to clear secretions, blood and foreign material.
2. Open the airway with a jaw thrust (when head or neck injury is suspected) or a head-tilt chin-lift.
3. Insert an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway to keep the airway open. Never use a nasopharyngeal airway when there is facial trauma.
4. Anticipate and prepare for endotracheal intubation if the airway cannot be maintained.
5. Immobilise the cervical spine in a neutral position, using a cervical collar and manual in-line support.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable points
points: 6. Give oxygen once the airway is open and assess for signs of airway obstruction such as stridor, gurgling or inability to speak.
7. Reassess the airway after every intervention.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Name each intervention and add its purpose or condition in a few words. The jaw thrust and the nasopharyngeal airway warning are the two details that earn the mark.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Primary Survey: Airway section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: stay within AIRWAY. Do not write oxygen by non-rebreather mask, chest dressings or IV fluids, which belong to Breathing and Circulation. Remember that a jaw thrust, not a head-tilt, is used when a neck injury is possible.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Airway always goes together with the cervical spine: 'A = Airway AND C-spine'.
Memory tip 2: Nasopharyngeal airway is forbidden in facial trauma. Say 'no NPA in a broken face'.
Memory tip 3: Move from the simplest to the most invasive: suction, manoeuvre, adjunct, tube.

aceItTip.title: Examiner Scoring Key & Common Pitfalls
tips: Marking rule: 1 mark per intervention. Write exactly five and make each one an action (suction, open, insert, prepare, immobilise).
Keywords the examiner looks for: suction, jaw thrust, head-tilt chin-lift, oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway, intubation, cervical spine immobilisation.
If a massive external haemorrhage is obvious, some guidelines control it first (C-ABCDE), but the notes follow ABCDE, so write the notes' order.
Related questions: 'state the interventions for breathing', 'for circulation', 'for disability' and 'components of the primary survey'. Use the same ABCDE frame for all of them.

questions.partTitle: Trauma Assessment: Primary and Secondary Survey
questions.text: Outline four (4) immediate nursing interventions for a patient with an open (sucking) chest wound.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Open chest wound and tension pneumothorax were tested in 3 past MCQs

askedIn.wording: Outline four (4) immediate nursing interventions for a patient with an open (sucking) chest wound.

modelAnswer.intro: An open (sucking) chest wound lets air enter the pleural space with each breath, so the lung collapses and breathing becomes laboured. The nurse treats it as a Breathing problem in the primary survey and acts at once.

subsections.heading: A. Four interventions to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Cover the wound with a non-occlusive (vented) dressing taped on three sides, so that air can escape from the chest but cannot be sucked in.
2. Give high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather mask at 10 to 15 L/min.
3. Assist ventilation with a bag-valve mask if breathing is inadequate.
4. Prepare for needle decompression or chest tube insertion if a tension pneumothorax develops.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable points
points: 5. Monitor SpO2 (a value below 95% is a concern) and respiratory rate, and attach a cardiac monitor.
6. Establish IV access and prepare for fluid resuscitation if there are signs of shock.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Start with the dressing, because it is the intervention the examiners look for. Always say 'on three sides'.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Primary Survey: Breathing section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: never seal the wound on all four sides, because this traps air and can cause a tension pneumothorax. The dressing is non-occlusive and taped on three sides.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Three sides taped, one side free: the free side works like a one-way flutter valve.
Memory tip 2: Think of what the lungs need first: a sealed-in-one-direction wound, then oxygen, then help with breathing, then a plan for pressure.
Memory tip 3: The April 2024 MCQ asked for exactly this: a vented dressing sealed on three sides.

mnemonics.summary: A home-made acrostic with one intervention per letter. It is a memory aid, not a published standard.
mnemonics.source: Original study aid built from the attached lecture notes

rows: Seal on three sides (non-occlusive, vented dressing)
Up the oxygen: NRM at 10 to 15 L/min
Keep ready for decompression or chest tube

aceItTip.title: Examiner Scoring Key & Common Pitfalls
tips: Marking rule: 1 mark per intervention, with the dressing as the key mark.
Keywords the examiner looks for: non-occlusive or vented dressing, three sides, oxygen by NRM, bag-valve mask, needle decompression, chest tube.
Do not write 'apply an airtight dressing'. It is unsafe and is marked wrong.
Related questions: 'manifestations of tension pneumothorax' (already asked) and 'management of tension pneumothorax' (needle decompression then chest tube).

questions.partTitle: Trauma Assessment: Primary and Secondary Survey
questions.text: Outline four (4) nursing interventions in the management of disability (D) in a trauma patient with a head injury.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · Disability is the least practised letter of ABCDE, so it is a likely 'gap' question

askedIn.wording: Outline four (4) nursing interventions in the management of disability (D) in a trauma patient with a head injury.

modelAnswer.intro: Disability is assessed with the AVPU scale or the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and by checking the pupils. A history of loss of consciousness suggests a significant head injury. The aim of care is to protect the brain from raised intracranial pressure (ICP) and low oxygen or blood pressure.

subsections.heading: A. Four interventions to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Raise the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees (if there is no spinal injury, or once the spine has been cleared or stabilised), to lower the ICP.
2. Maintain a systolic blood pressure above 100 mmHg and an oxygen saturation above 90%, to keep the brain perfused and oxygenated.
3. Prepare mannitol for raised ICP.
4. Reduce external stimuli (noise, light and unnecessary handling).

subsections.heading: B. Assessment points that support the answer
points: 5. Assess the level of consciousness with AVPU or GCS and check the pupils for size, equality and reaction.
6. Concerns to report: low GCS, unequal or sluggish pupils, one-sided weakness and abnormal posturing.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Give the number with each intervention (30 to 45 degrees, SBP above 100, SpO2 above 90%), because the numbers are what the examiner marks.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Primary Survey: Disability section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: the question asks for interventions. Do not spend your marks only on assessment (AVPU, GCS), which is the 'how to check', not the 'what to do'.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: The numbers: 30-45 for the bed angle, 100 for the systolic pressure, 90 for the saturation.
Memory tip 2: Head up lowers the pressure inside the head, the same logic as sitting up for a headache or a nosebleed.
Memory tip 3: AVPU: Alert, Verbal, Pain, Unresponsive. It is the fastest check of the level of consciousness.

aceItTip.title: Examiner Scoring Key & Common Pitfalls
tips: Marking rule: 1 mark per intervention. Write four, each with its number or purpose.
Keywords the examiner looks for: head of bed 30 to 45 degrees, SBP above 100, SpO2 above 90%, mannitol, reduce stimuli.
Do not raise the head of the bed if a spinal injury has not been excluded. The notes add 'if no spinal injury or once stabilised'.
Related question: 'outline the interventions for exposure': remove all clothing to find hidden injuries and prevent hypothermia.

questions.partTitle: Trauma Assessment: Primary and Secondary Survey
questions.text: State five (5) investigations that may be done during the secondary survey of a trauma patient.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · The secondary survey has been tested as an SAQ (history) and is the natural next question

askedIn.wording: State five (5) investigations that may be done during the secondary survey of a trauma patient.

modelAnswer.intro: The secondary survey is a systematic head-to-toe examination done after the primary survey and life-saving interventions. Investigations help to find injuries that were not obvious at first. They are grouped into laboratory tests and imaging.

subsections.heading: A. Five investigations to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Group and cross-match (or screen), to prepare blood in case of haemorrhage.
2. Full blood count, to assess blood loss and anaemia.
3. Bedside glucose, because low glucose can mimic or worsen a head injury.
4. Chest X-ray and pelvic X-ray, to find chest injuries and pelvic fractures.
5. FAST (focused assessment with sonography for trauma) or CT of the head and C-spine, to find internal bleeding or head and neck injuries.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable investigations
points: 6. Electrolytes and renal function, urinalysis and a pregnancy test (in women of reproductive age).
7. Ethanol level and toxicology screen, and clotting studies.
8. Lactate and base deficit, as markers of shock; MRI where indicated.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Mix laboratory tests and imaging so that the answer covers both groups. Name each test and, where possible, give its purpose.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Secondary Survey section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not include the steps of the head-to-toe examination or the interventions (NG tube, catheter, splints) from the same section. They are separate parts of the secondary survey.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Group the list by body fluid: blood, sugar, salts, urine, toxins, then pictures.
Memory tip 2: The trauma imaging trio is chest, pelvis and FAST.
Memory tip 3: The secondary survey has six parts in order: history, head-to-toe, vital signs, labs, imaging, other interventions. Say 'H-H-V-L-I-O'.

aceItTip.title: Examiner Scoring Key & Common Pitfalls
tips: Marking rule: 1 mark per investigation. Five different tests, mixing lab and imaging.
Keywords the examiner looks for: group and cross-match, FBC, glucose, electrolytes, urinalysis, pregnancy test, chest X-ray, pelvic X-ray, CT, FAST.
Never list two forms of the same test as separate points, for example 'X-ray of chest' and 'chest radiograph'.
Always state that the secondary survey starts only after the primary survey and life-saving interventions are complete.

parts.title: Shock
parts.frequencyBadge: Predicted: Very High · MCQs in every paper, SAQs not yet set
parts.description: Early signs, management of hypovolaemic and anaphylactic shock, and the four types of shock.

questions.text: State five (5) early signs of hypovolaemic shock.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Very High · 'Early sign of shock' was an MCQ in 2 of 5 papers

askedIn.wording: State five (5) early signs of hypovolaemic shock.

modelAnswer.intro: Shock is a clinical syndrome from inadequate tissue perfusion, which creates an imbalance between oxygen and nutrient delivery and cellular needs. In hypovolaemic shock, fluid or blood loss lowers preload, stroke volume and cardiac output. The body compensates at first, so the EARLY signs reflect compensation, not collapse.

subsections.heading: A. Five early signs to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Anxiety, restlessness, agitation or combativeness (neurological, from reduced cerebral perfusion).
2. Tachycardia, the compensatory rise in heart rate to maintain cardiac output.
3. Tachypnoea or air hunger with a falling SpO2.
4. Pallor with delayed capillary refill.
5. Reduced urine output.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable early signs
points: 6. Thirst, nausea and abdominal pain (gastrointestinal).
7. Mean arterial pressure below 60 mmHg and a lactate above 2 mmol/L.
8. Diaphoresis (sweating).

modelAnswer.conclusion: Late signs to avoid in this answer: hypotension and bradycardia, anuria, absent bowel sounds, dilated pupils, central cyanosis, unresponsiveness, mottled skin and a lactate above 4 mmol/L.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Hypovolaemic Shock section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: hypotension is a LATE sign, because the body keeps the blood pressure up for as long as it can. A student who writes hypotension, anuria or unconsciousness has described late shock and loses the marks.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Early shock is the body fighting: fast, restless, pale, thirsty and passing little urine.
Memory tip 2: Late shock is the body losing: slow, quiet, grey, mottled and not passing urine at all.
Memory tip 3: The April 2024 MCQ asked for the early sign of shock: the answer was tachycardia, not hypotension and not anuria.

questions.text: Outline five (5) nursing interventions in the management of hypovolaemic shock.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Very High · Hypovolaemic shock is the most common shock in trauma and was tested in the MCQs in 2024 and 2025

askedIn.wording: Outline five (5) nursing interventions in the management of hypovolaemic shock.

modelAnswer.intro: The aims of treatment are to stop the loss of blood or fluid, restore the circulating volume and oxygen delivery, and monitor the response.

subsections.heading: A. Five interventions to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Control the bleeding with direct pressure or surgery.
2. Give high-flow oxygen.
3. Insert large-bore IV access (16G or larger) and send blood for FBC, U&E, creatinine, group and cross-match and glucose.
4. Give a normal saline bolus (500 to 1000 mL in adults, 10 mL/kg in children, over 5 to 20 minutes) and blood products as indicated.
5. Put the patient on an ECG monitor with pulse oximetry, record vital signs every 15 to 30 minutes, and insert a urinary catheter to monitor hourly urine output.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable interventions
points: 6. Prevent hypothermia, splint large bone injuries (femur, pelvis) and insert a gastric tube to prevent distension, vomiting and aspiration.
7. Arrange imaging: chest X-ray, CT head and neck, pelvic X-ray and FAST.
8. If there is a thermal injury, stop the burning process.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Include the numbers (16G, 500 to 1000 mL, 10 mL/kg, hourly urine) because they distinguish a strong answer from a general one.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Hypovolaemic Shock section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not write the management of cardiogenic shock (diuretics, vasodilators, dobutamine). In hypovolaemic shock the patient needs volume, not less volume.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: The sequence mirrors a leaking tank: plug the hole, give oxygen, open two big lines, refill the tank, and watch the gauges (monitor and urine).
Memory tip 2: Fluid bolus numbers: 500-1000 mL in adults and 10 mL/kg in children.
Memory tip 3: Hypovolaemic patients are thirsty and need fluid; cardiogenic patients are waterlogged and need the opposite. Do not mix them up.

questions.text: Outline five (5) nursing interventions in the management of a patient with anaphylactic shock.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Very High · Anaphylaxis was tested in the MCQs in 3 of 5 papers (April 2024, September 2024 and April 2025) and has not yet been set as an SAQ

askedIn.wording: Outline five (5) nursing interventions in the management of a patient with anaphylactic shock.

modelAnswer.intro: Anaphylaxis is an acute, life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction. Triggers include shellfish, peanuts, bee stings, penicillin, latex and iodine contrast. Death can occur from airway swelling or circulatory collapse within minutes, so treatment is immediate.

subsections.heading: A. Five interventions to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Remove the causative agent and secure the airway (intubate if needed, because of upper airway oedema).
2. Give intramuscular epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) into the mid-anterolateral thigh. Document the time. It can be repeated in 5 to 15 minutes.
3. Give high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather mask at 10 to 15 L/min.
4. Obtain IV access and, for hypotension, give 1 to 2 L of 0.9% saline (5 to 10 mL/kg in the first 5 to 10 minutes).
5. Give an inhaled beta-2 agonist (albuterol) for bronchospasm, and antihistamines as an adjunct.

subsections.heading: B. Recognition and other points
points: 6. Signs: dyspnoea, cough, throat tightness, stridor, wheeze, urticaria, angioedema of the lips and tongue, syncope, palpitations, hypotension and tachycardia.
7. Respiratory and cardiopulmonary arrest can follow, so be ready to start CPR.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Epinephrine is the first-line drug and antihistamines are only adjuncts. Put epinephrine first in your answer.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Anaphylactic Shock section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: antihistamines, steroids and fluids do not replace epinephrine. A student who gives an oral antihistamine as the first intervention loses the key mark. The correct route is IM, not IV, and the correct site is the mid-anterolateral thigh.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Epinephrine goes into the muscle of the outer thigh because absorption there is faster than from the arm or under the skin.
Memory tip 2: The dose pair: 0.01 mg/kg of the 1:1000 strength (1 mg/mL). For a 20 kg child that is 0.2 mg or 0.2 mL.
Memory tip 3: Airway swelling is the killer, so the airway and oxygen move alongside the drug, not after it.
Memory tip 4: Repeat the epinephrine after 5 to 15 minutes if the patient has not improved.

questions.text: Name the four (4) types of shock and state one cause of each.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · 'Types of shock' and 'cause of cardiogenic shock' were tested in the MCQs in 2024 and 2025

askedIn.wording: Name the four (4) types of shock and state one cause of each.

modelAnswer.intro: Shock needs four intact components to maintain perfusion: the vessels, an adequate intravascular volume, adequate gas exchange in the lungs and a functioning heart. A failure in any one of them gives one of the four types of shock.

subsections.heading: A. Four types and a cause of each (1 mark each)
points: 1. Hypovolaemic shock: loss of blood or fluid, for example haemorrhage from trauma, burns or severe diarrhoea.
2. Cardiogenic shock: failure of the heart as a pump, for example myocardial infarction, dysrhythmias or cardiomyopathy.
3. Distributive shock: vasodilation or pooling of blood, for example anaphylactic, septic or neurogenic shock.
4. Obstructive shock: a physical blockage to blood flow, for example cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism or tension pneumothorax.

subsections.heading: B. Key differences worth knowing
points: 5. Neurogenic shock is the one with bradycardia, hypotension and warm, dry, flushed skin, usually from a spinal cord injury.
6. Septic shock is the most common distributive shock and the last, most severe stage of sepsis.
7. Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume (about 5 L/min at rest).

modelAnswer.conclusion: Give the type, a one-line mechanism and one cause for each so that each mark is secure.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Types of Shock section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: anaphylactic, septic and neurogenic shock are not separate types; they are the three subtypes of DISTRIBUTIVE shock. Do not list them as four of the types.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Tank, pump, pipes, blockage: Hypovolaemic is the tank, cardiogenic the pump, distributive the pipes and obstructive the blockage.
Memory tip 2: A second hook is HCDO: Hypovolaemic, Cardiogenic, Distributive, Obstructive.
Memory tip 3: Tension pneumothorax and tamponade are obstructive because they stop blood from returning to or leaving the heart.

mnemonics.summary: A plumbing analogy that is widely used in nursing teaching. Use it to recall mechanism and cause together.
mnemonics.source: Widely used student analogy for classifying shock; lecture notes (types of shock)

mnemonics.title: Key clue for each type
mnemonics.summary: Short clue words that help in MCQs and in the SAQ.

rows: Thirst, cool pale skin, falling urine output
Chest pain or crackles, a failed pump (diuretics and dobutamine)
Bradycardia with warm, dry skin after a spinal injury
Raised neck veins; relieve the obstruction

tips: Marking rule: 1 mark per type with its cause. Do not repeat the same cause.
Keywords the examiner looks for: hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive (with anaphylactic, septic or neurogenic), obstructive, and a correct cause for each.
If asked for 'subtypes of distributive shock', write anaphylactic, neurogenic and septic.

questions.text: State five (5) components of high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in an adult.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · CPR numbers were tested in the MCQs in 4 of 5 papers and have never been set as an SAQ

askedIn.wording: State five (5) components of high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in an adult.

modelAnswer.intro: CPR is the external maintenance of circulation and respiration through chest compressions and artificial ventilation. Its quality decides survival: each minute of delayed resuscitation reduces survival by about 10%.

subsections.heading: A. Five components to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
2. Depth of at least 5 cm (2 inches), with the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum, the other hand on top, arms straight and shoulders over the hands.
3. Allow full chest recoil after every compression.
4. Minimise interruptions: keep any pause to less than 10 seconds.
5. Use a compression to ventilation ratio of 30:2, and swap compressors every 2 minutes (switch in under 5 seconds) to avoid fatigue.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable points
points: 6. The victim lies supine on a firm, flat surface with the chest exposed.
7. Reassess the pulse and breathing every 2 minutes (5 cycles).
8. Give each breath over 1 second with visible chest rise.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Give the number with each component: 100 to 120, 5 cm, 10 seconds, 30:2 and 2 minutes.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Adult CPR section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: 'High quality' means the technique, not the sequence. Do not write Safety, Stimulate, Shout, Check pulse, which is the BLS sequence and a different question.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Fast, deep, let it rise, do not stop, swap: that is the entire CPR quality checklist.
Memory tip 2: The numbers: 100-120, 5 cm, 30:2, 10 seconds, 2 minutes.
Memory tip 3: The compressor swaps every 2 minutes, which is also when the pulse is rechecked.

questions.text: State the five (5) links in the adult chain of survival.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · The chain of survival was an MCQ in 2 of 5 papers (September 2023 and September 2024)

askedIn.wording: State the five (5) links in the adult chain of survival.

modelAnswer.intro: The chain of survival is the series of actions that, performed in order and without delay, give a person in sudden cardiac arrest the best chance of survival.

subsections.heading: A. Five links to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Early recognition of cardiac arrest.
2. Activation of emergency medical services (EMS).
3. Early CPR.
4. Early defibrillation, within 3 to 5 minutes of collapse.
5. Early advanced care.

subsections.heading: B. Useful extra points
points: 6. Each minute of delay in resuscitation reduces survival by about 10%.
7. The paediatric chain is: prevention, early recognition, prompt EMS call, high-quality CPR, rapid defibrillation and advanced care, and integrated post-cardiac-arrest care.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write the links in the correct order. The order is tested in the MCQs.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Chain of Survival section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not confuse the adult chain, which starts with recognition, with the paediatric chain, which starts with prevention.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Recognise, Alert, Compress, Defibrillate, Advance: each link triggers the next.
Memory tip 2: The shock is delivered early (3 to 5 minutes) because the heart rhythm can only be corrected while it is still shockable.
Memory tip 3: Adult: recognition is first. Paediatric: prevention is first, because most child arrests are respiratory and preventable.

questions.text: A 60 kg adult has burns covering 40% of the total body surface area (TBSA). Using the Parkland formula, calculate (a) the total volume of fluid for the first 24 hours, (b) the volume to be given in the first 8 hours and the hourly rate, and (c) the volume for the next 16 hours.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Parkland appeared in the 2025 MCQs and the burn phase was set as an SAQ

askedIn.wording: A 60 kg adult has burns covering 40% of the total body surface area (TBSA). Using the Parkland formula, calculate (a) the total volume of fluid for the first 24 hours, (b) the volume to be given in the first 8 hours and the hourly rate, and (c) the volume for the next 16 hours.

modelAnswer.intro: The Parkland formula is used when the burn is larger than 20% TBSA. Ringer's lactate is given at 4 mL x % TBSA x weight in kg over 24 hours. Half is given in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn, and the other half over the next 16 hours.

subsections.heading: A. Working to write (show each step)
points: 1. Total in 24 hours = 4 mL x 40 x 60 kg = 9,600 mL of Ringer's lactate.
2. First 8 hours = 9,600 / 2 = 4,800 mL, which is 4,800 / 8 = 600 mL per hour.
3. Next 16 hours = 4,800 mL, which is 4,800 / 16 = 300 mL per hour.

subsections.heading: B. Points that protect the marks
points: 4. The 8 hours are counted from the time of the burn, not from the time of arrival.
5. Adjust the rate to the response and aim for a urine output of at least 30 mL per hour in adults.
6. The modified Parkland formula uses 3 mL x % TBSA x weight (kg) of Hartmann's solution with the same split.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write the formula first, substitute the numbers, then give the answer with its units (mL and mL/hour).
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Burns: Fluid Resuscitation section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: read what the question asks. A first-8-hours question wants half of the 24-hour total, not the whole of it. The 2025 MCQ with the 50 kg patient (27%) had 5,400 mL as a distractor.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Four times weight times percent, half now, half later: 4 x kg x %.
Memory tip 2: Half in the first 8 hours, half over the next 16 hours. Hourly rate = half divided by 8 for the first period and by 16 for the second.
Memory tip 3: Always check that the burn is above 20% TBSA before applying the formula.

mnemonics.title: Parkland worked examples (study aid)
mnemonics.summary: Practice until the steps are automatic: weight x % x 4, divide by 2, divide by 8.
mnemonics.source: Lecture notes (worked examples) and this question

mnemonics.title: Rule of Nines (adult TBSA)
mnemonics.summary: Used to estimate the percentage before the formula is applied. Use Lund and Browder for children.

aceItTip.title: Examiner Scoring Key & Common Pitfalls
tips: Marking rule: marks are given for the formula, the substitution and the correct answers with units. Show every line.
Keywords the examiner looks for: Parkland, 4 mL x %TBSA x weight, Ringer's lactate, half in 8 hours, half in 16 hours, urine output 30 mL/hour.
Always check which period is requested: first 8 hours, next 16 hours or the whole 24 hours.

questions.text: Outline five (5) first aid measures at the scene for a patient with a thermal burn.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · First aid is the newest SAQ trend (seizures, 2025) and burn scene care is a whole lecture section

askedIn.wording: Outline five (5) first aid measures at the scene for a patient with a thermal burn.

modelAnswer.intro: First aid for burns stops the burning process, limits tissue damage and protects the patient until medical care is reached. Treat every burn as potentially life-threatening until it has been assessed.

subsections.heading: A. Five measures to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Stop the burning process: extinguish flames (stop, drop and roll, or smother with a blanket) and disconnect electrical sources.
2. Cool the burn by soaking in cool running water for 10 to 15 minutes. Do not exceed this because of the risk of hypothermia.
3. Remove restrictive items such as jewellery, piercings and clothing (adherent clothing may stay once cooled) to prevent constriction from oedema.
4. Cover the wound with a clean, dry, loose dressing, to reduce contamination, keep the patient warm and reduce pain.
5. Transfer to hospital without delay. For a chemical burn, brush off the chemical, remove clothes and irrigate continuously with water.

subsections.heading: B. What NOT to do
points: 6. Do not use ice, do not apply butter or greasy substances, do not break blisters and do not delay medical help.
7. Standing still makes the person breathe flames and smoke, and running fans the flames, so use stop, drop and roll.

modelAnswer.conclusion: List the actions in the order in which they are done at the scene.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Burns: First Aid section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: this is SCENE first aid, not hospital care. Do not write the Parkland formula, urinary catheters or IV morphine. Do not use ice.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Stop the fire, cool the burn, take off the tight items, cover it, and carry the patient to hospital.
Memory tip 2: The cooling time is 10 to 15 minutes. Longer causes hypothermia.
Memory tip 3: Nothing greasy and nothing icy: butter and ice are both wrong.

questions.text: State five (5) clues that suggest an inhalation injury in a burn patient.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · Inhalation injury accounts for 10 to 20% of burn centre admissions and is the main cause of death at fire scenes

askedIn.wording: State five (5) clues that suggest an inhalation injury in a burn patient.

modelAnswer.intro: Inhalation injury is caused by superheated air and noxious gases such as carbon monoxide. It makes the airway swell, so early recognition and early intubation save lives.

subsections.heading: A. Five clues to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. A history of a fire in an enclosed space.
2. Facial or neck burns.
3. Singed nasal hair.
4. Hoarseness or stridor.
5. Sooty or bloody sputum.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable clues and the action
points: 6. Tachypnoea and hypoxaemia.
7. Oral or pharyngeal blistering.
8. Action: early intubation is advised for upper airway injury because the oedema progresses.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write the clues the nurse can see or hear at the bedside. Add one line about early intubation if there is space.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Burns: Inhalation Injury section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: clues are findings, not interventions. Do not spend the five marks on oxygen or fluids.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Look at the face, listen to the voice, smell the smoke, and examine the sputum.
Memory tip 2: Hoarseness and stridor mean the airway is already narrowing, so call for help and prepare to intubate.
Memory tip 3: Carbon monoxide poisoning gives a normal-looking colour but a very sick patient.

questions.text: Describe Curling's ulcer, stating its cause, two (2) clinical manifestations and two (2) preventive measures.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · Curling's ulcer was an MCQ in April 2025

askedIn.wording: Describe Curling's ulcer, stating its cause, two (2) clinical manifestations and two (2) preventive measures.

modelAnswer.intro: Curling's ulcer is a duodenal erosion that develops within 24 hours of a major burn (more than 20% TBSA) because the stomach and duodenal lining lose their blood supply.

subsections.heading: A. Four points to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Cause: mucosal ischaemia of the gut caused by hypovolaemia and the stress response after the burn.
2. Clinical manifestation: occult blood in the stool.
3. Clinical manifestation: 'coffee-ground' vomit or bloody vomitus.
4. Prevention: an H2 blocker or a proton pump inhibitor, with mucoprotectants such as sucralfate, and early enteral feeding.

subsections.heading: B. Related points
points: 5. Paralytic ileus is a separate GI complication, with reduced bowel sounds, distension, nausea and vomiting. It is treated with gastric decompression (NG tube).
6. Patients with more than 20% burns are prone to gastric mucosal damage.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Cover the four parts: cause, two signs and prevention.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Burns: Curling's Ulcer section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not describe paralytic ileus as the signs of Curling's ulcer. Gastric distension and vomiting are ileus; occult blood and coffee-ground vomit are Curling's ulcer. Ranitidine, named in some slides, is withdrawn in many countries, so write 'H2 blocker or PPI'.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Curling is a Burn ulcer; it Bleeds.
Memory tip 2: Occult blood in the stool plus coffee-ground vomit is the whole sign list.
Memory tip 3: Prevent it by cutting acid and feeding the gut early.

questions.text: Outline five (5) first aid measures for a person with severe external bleeding.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · First aid SAQ (seizures) appeared in April 2025 and bleeding is the first item in the first aid lecture

askedIn.wording: Outline five (5) first aid measures for a person with severe external bleeding.

modelAnswer.intro: Severe loss of blood leads to shock. First aid aims to stop the bleeding, keep the person calm and warm, and get medical help quickly.

subsections.heading: A. Five measures to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Call emergency help if the bleeding is severe or the wound is large.
2. Apply firm direct pressure with a clean cloth or dressing.
3. Elevate the limb above the level of the heart.
4. Do not remove soaked dressings; add more dressings on top, because removal disrupts clotting.
5. Keep the person warm and calm to prevent shock, and monitor breathing and consciousness.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable points
points: 6. Apply pressure at a pressure point if trained.
7. Use a tourniquet above the wound for severe limb bleeding if trained.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Start with direct pressure, because it is the key action.

askedIn.wording: State what each letter of the acronym FAST stands for and outline two (2) other first aid measures for a person with a suspected stroke.

modelAnswer.intro: Stroke is either ischaemic (about 85%, from a blocked artery) or haemorrhagic (about 15%, from a burst vessel). The warning signs are recognised with the acronym FAST.

subsections.heading: A. FAST (4 marks) and two measures (1 mark)
points: 1. F: Face drooping.
2. A: Arm weakness.
3. S: Speech difficulty.
4. T: Time to call emergency services.
5. Activate EMS, reassure the patient, use the recovery position if unconscious and start CPR if unresponsive.

subsections.heading: B. Hospital treatment (extra)
points: 6. IV alteplase is the drug of choice for ischaemic stroke within 3 hours; thrombectomy can remove the clot; surgery is used for haemorrhagic stroke.
7. Risk factors: hypertension (leading cause), smoking, heavy alcohol use, diabetes, high cholesterol and stress or depression.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write each letter with its word, then the two actions.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Stroke section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: S stands for Speech difficulty, not slowed breathing or seizures. T is Time to call, not 'treatment'.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Face, Arm, Speech, Time: check them in that order.
Memory tip 2: Eighty-five blocked, fifteen burst.
Memory tip 3: Three hours is the alteplase window.

questions.text: Outline the first aid management of a patient with hypoglycaemia.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · Diabetic emergencies are a full table in the first aid lecture

askedIn.wording: Outline the first aid management of a patient with hypoglycaemia.

modelAnswer.intro: Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) is caused by a missed meal, too little food, extra exercise, vomiting or too much medication. Signs include weakness, hunger, confusion, sweating with cold clammy skin, rapid pulse, palpitations and trembling.

subsections.heading: A. Three points to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Rest the patient and give something sugary if the patient is alert.
2. Call for help if the patient is not improving. If the patient is not fully alert, do not feed because of the risk of choking.
3. If the patient is unresponsive, open the airway, check breathing and prepare for CPR.

subsections.heading: B. How to tell it from hyperglycaemia
points: 4. Hypoglycaemia gives cold, clammy skin and a rapid pulse. Hyperglycaemia gives warm, dry skin, fruity breath, excessive thirst and rapid breathing.
5. For hyperglycaemia call for emergency help, check for a medical bracelet or card and monitor breathing and pulse.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Keep to the actions. Do not write the long list of causes.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Diabetic Emergencies section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: never put food or drink into the mouth of a patient who is not fully alert.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Cold and clammy, give candy; hot and dry, sugar is high.
Memory tip 2: Alert gets sugar; drowsy gets airway; unresponsive gets CPR.

questions.text: State four (4) signs of a significant head injury.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · Head injury links with the disability step of the primary survey

askedIn.wording: State four (4) signs of a significant head injury.

modelAnswer.intro: A head injury may be open (a bleeding wound) or closed (no visible injury). A history of loss of consciousness suggests a significant head injury.

subsections.heading: A. Four signs to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Altered consciousness, which may improve and then deteriorate.
2. Clear fluid (CSF) from the ears or nose, suggesting a basal skull fracture.
3. Black eyes and bruising behind the ears.
4. Pupil or vision changes (dilated pupils, double or blurred vision).

subsections.heading: B. Other signs and first aid
points: 5. Skull deformity, nausea and vomiting.

6. First aid: do not move the person unless in immediate danger, monitor airway and breathing, minimise head and neck movement, control scalp bleeding with direct pressure and start CPR if breathing or pulse stops.

modelAnswer.conclusion: State the sign and, if you can, what it suggests.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Head Injury section).

questions.text: Outline the management of a conscious infant with a foreign body airway obstruction and an ineffective cough.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · Infant FBAO was an MCQ in April 2024 and paediatric CPR ratios in April 2025

askedIn.wording: Outline the management of a conscious infant with a foreign body airway obstruction and an ineffective cough.

modelAnswer.intro: Back slaps, chest thrusts and abdominal thrusts all raise the pressure inside the chest and can expel the object.

subsections.heading: A. Four steps to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. If the cough is effective, encourage coughing and monitor for deterioration. If it is ineffective, act at once.
2. Hold the infant face-down along the forearm with the head lower than the body and give 5 back slaps.
3. Turn the infant upright on the thigh and give 5 chest thrusts with 2 to 3 fingers; check the airway and repeat.
4. If the infant becomes unconscious, open the airway, give 5 breaths and start CPR.

subsections.heading: B. Related points
points: 5. For a child over 1 year, kneel behind and give 5 abdominal thrusts, repeating until the object comes out.
6. Signs of severe obstruction: silent cough, inability to cry, stridor, cyanosis.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Say 5 and 5.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Paediatric FBAO section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: never give abdominal thrusts to an infant.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Five slaps, five thrusts, look, repeat.
Memory tip 2: Under 1: back and chest. Over 1: belly.

questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium · Paediatric anatomy is a listed section of the notes

askedIn.wording: State four (4) anatomical differences in children that make airway management difficult.

modelAnswer.intro: Children are not small adults. Their anatomy makes the airway easy to block.

subsections.heading: A. Four differences to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Smaller upper and lower airways and a smaller sub-glottic airway.
2. In infants, a relatively large tongue obstructs the airway easily.
3. A large occiput, so the sniffing position may obstruct the airway.
4. Limited oxygen reserve.

subsections.heading: B. Other differences
points: 5. Large abdominal organs, especially in infants.
6. A larger surface-area-to-volume ratio than adults.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Give the feature and its effect.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Paediatric Airway section).

askedIn.wording: State the three (3) components of the Paediatric Assessment Triangle and one abnormal finding for each.

modelAnswer.intro: The Paediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT) is the initial 'critical look' at a child. It forms a general impression and sets the urgency of intervention.

subsections.heading: A. Three components (1 mark each)
points: 1. Appearance: abnormal finding is a weak or absent cry, decreased responsiveness or floppy tone.
2. Work of breathing: abnormal finding is nasal flaring, retractions, tracheal tug or noisy breathing.
3. Circulation to skin: abnormal finding is cyanosis, mottling or pallor, or capillary refill over 2 seconds.

points: 4. Normal capillary refill is 2 seconds or less.

questions.text: Outline five (5) hospital management measures for a poisoned patient.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · Organophosphate poisoning was an SAQ in September 2023 and the antidote table is long

askedIn.wording: Outline five (5) hospital management measures for a poisoned patient.

modelAnswer.intro: Poisoning is the inhalation, ingestion, absorption, injection or skin or mucous membrane contact with a toxic substance.

subsections.heading: A. Five measures to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Support airway, breathing and circulation and give oxygen.
2. Obtain IV access and infuse Ringer's lactate or normal saline; start continuous cardiac monitoring.
3. Check the glucose and, if it is low, give dextrose 50% 50 mL IV.
4. Decontaminate: activated charcoal, most effective within 1 hour; gastric lavage useful within 1 to 4 hours.
5. Give the specific antidote, and benzodiazepines for agitation or seizures.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable measures
points: 6. Thiamine 50 to 100 mg IV in suspected chronic alcohol abuse.
7. Naloxone 0.4 to 2 mg for suspected opioid exposure; haemodialysis in severe cases.
8. Monitor urine output and repeat electrolytes, vital signs and neurological status.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Name the measure and its timing where one is given.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Poisoning: Hospital Management section).

questions.text: Outline five (5) key features of the triage process.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Very High · Triage was an SAQ in 4 of 5 past papers; the process section has not been asked yet

askedIn.wording: Outline five (5) key features of the triage process.

modelAnswer.intro: The triage process is the brief, structured interview and assessment the triage nurse carries out when the patient arrives. Its purpose is to find life threats at once and to assign a severity rating.

subsections.heading: A. Five features to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. The assessment is brief and timely: the goal is an initial triage assessment within 5 minutes of arrival.
2. If a life-threatening airway, breathing or circulation problem is found, interventions start immediately and the patient is moved to a care area.
3. The chief complaint is documented in the patient's own words, in quotation marks.
4. The nurse is non-judgmental and empathetic towards the patient.
5. For a trauma patient, the mechanism and pattern of injury are documented.

subsections.heading: B. Other acceptable features
points: 6. Assessment tools are used: PQRST for pain and SAMPLE for history.
7. Triage vital signs are taken: AVPU, pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure, temperature and SpO2.
8. A severity rating (acuity level) is assigned at the end of the assessment.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write short statements that describe how the process is carried out, using the figures in the notes (5 minutes) and the phrase 'in the patient's own words'.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Triage Process section).

questions.text: State what each letter of the PQRST tool stands for when assessing a patient's pain during triage.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Very High · The 'P' of PQRST was an MCQ in September 2024; the full tool has never been set as an SAQ

askedIn.wording: State what each letter of the PQRST tool stands for when assessing a patient's pain during triage.

modelAnswer.intro: PQRST is the assessment tool used at triage to describe pain. It gives the nurse a quick and structured picture of the pain so that the severity rating is accurate.

subsections.heading: A. Five letters to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. P: Provokes or Palliates, meaning what makes the pain worse and what relieves it.
2. Q: Quality, meaning what the pain feels like (for example sharp, dull, crushing or burning).
3. R: Region or Radiation, meaning where the pain is and whether it spreads elsewhere.
4. S: Severity, meaning how bad the pain is on a scale such as 0 to 10.
5. T: Time, meaning when it started, how long it has lasted and whether it is constant or comes and goes.

subsections.heading: B. How the tool is used
points: 6. The pain score helps to assign the CTAS level: pain 8 to 10 out of 10 is level 2, 4 to 7 is level 3 and 0 to 3 is level 4.
7. PQRST is used together with SAMPLE, which is the tool for the history.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write the letter, the word and a few words of meaning for each line.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (PQRST Pain Assessment section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: the P is Provokes (or Palliates), not Precipitating, Position or Past history. Those were the wrong options in the 2024 MCQ.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Ask five questions in order: what Provokes it, what is the Quality, which Region, how Severe, what Time?
Memory tip 2: The pain score links to the CTAS levels: 8 to 10 is emergent, 4 to 7 is urgent and 0 to 3 is less urgent.
Memory tip 3: PQRST is for pain; SAMPLE is for history. Do not mix them.

questions.text: Outline the five (5) levels of the Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS), stating the category and the maximum time to be seen by a doctor for each.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Very High · CTAS levels were tested in the MCQs in every one of the 5 papers

askedIn.wording: Outline the five (5) levels of the Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS), stating the category and the maximum time to be seen by a doctor for each.

modelAnswer.intro: The Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS) sorts patients into five levels. Each level has a category, a colour and a time within which the patient must be seen by a doctor.

subsections.heading: A. Five levels to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Level 1, Resuscitation (blue): seen immediately (0 minutes).
2. Level 2, Emergent (red): seen in under 15 minutes.
3. Level 3, Urgent (yellow): seen in under 30 minutes.
4. Level 4, Less urgent (green): seen within 1 hour.
5. Level 5, Non-urgent (white): seen within 2 hours.

subsections.heading: B. One example per level to anchor the answer
points: 6. Level 1: cardiac or respiratory arrest, shock, BP below 90/60, SpO2 below 90%, GCS 3 to 8, anaphylaxis, status epilepticus.
7. Level 2: overdose with stable vitals, pain 8 to 10 out of 10, moderate asthma, severe abdominal pain, assault or abuse.
8. Level 3: mild asthma, pain 4 to 7 out of 10, vomiting or diarrhoea with dehydration.
9. Level 4: minor soft-tissue trauma, headache, earache, pain 0 to 3 out of 10.
10. Level 5: sore throat or URTI without fever, diarrhoea or vomiting alone without dehydration.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Put the level, the category and the time on one line so that each mark is clear.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (CTAS section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: level 2 is 'under 15 minutes' and level 3 is 'under 30 minutes'. Students often swap them. Level 4 is 'within 1 hour' and level 5 is 'within 2 hours'.

Memory tip 2: The colours go Blue, Red, Yellow, Green, White. 'Big Red Yellow Giraffes Wander'.

askedIn.wording: Assign the correct CTAS level and the maximum time to be seen by a doctor for each of the following patients: (a) a patient with severe respiratory distress and SpO2 of 85%; (b) an adult with a drug overdose and stable vital signs; (c) a child with mild asthma; (d) an adult with a minor soft-tissue injury and pain of 2 out of 10; (e) an adult with a sore throat without fever.

modelAnswer.intro: Application questions give a clinical picture and ask for the level. Match the key finding (a vital sign, a pain score or a diagnosis) to the table.

subsections.heading: A. Five answers to write (1 mark each)
points: (a) Level 1, Resuscitation: seen immediately, because SpO2 below 90% and severe respiratory distress are level 1 findings.
(b) Level 2, Emergent: seen in under 15 minutes, because overdose with stable vital signs is level 2.
(c) Level 3, Urgent: seen in under 30 minutes, because mild asthma is level 3.
(d) Level 4, Less urgent: seen within 1 hour, because minor soft-tissue trauma and pain of 0 to 3 out of 10 are level 4.
(e) Level 5, Non-urgent: seen within 2 hours, because a sore throat without fever is level 5.

subsections.heading: B. Reminder of related findings from the notes
points: 6. Moderate asthma is level 2, whereas mild asthma is level 3.
7. Pain 8 to 10 out of 10 is level 2, pain 4 to 7 out of 10 is level 3.
8. A BP below 90/60 or a GCS of 3 to 8 is level 1.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Give the level, the category and the time for each patient.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (CTAS Application section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: mild and moderate asthma sit in different levels (3 and 2). A stable overdose is level 2, but an unconscious overdose with GCS 3 to 8 is level 1.

questions.text: Define the following terms: (a) medical emergency, (b) multidisciplinary team, (c) physical trauma.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Definitions open the notes and are easy 3-mark questions

askedIn.wording: Define the following terms: (a) medical emergency, (b) multidisciplinary team, (c) physical trauma.

modelAnswer.intro: Definition questions test whether you can state the meaning clearly in one sentence. Learn the exact wording in the notes.

subsections.heading: A. Three definitions to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Medical emergency: a sudden injury or serious illness that, if not treated right away, could cause death or serious harm.
2. Multidisciplinary team: a group of professionals from different specialties who collaborate toward a common goal. The emergency nurse is one member of that team.
3. Physical trauma: a serious injury to the body. The two main types are blunt force and sharp force (penetrating) trauma.

subsections.heading: B. Related definitions
points: 4. Blunt force trauma: the victim hits, or is hit by, a hard object.
5. Sharp force or penetrating trauma: the victim is poked, cut or stabbed, and an object pierces the skin, usually creating an open wound.

modelAnswer.conclusion: One clear sentence per term. Do not add extra information.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Definitions section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not define a medical emergency as 'any illness'. The key words are 'sudden', 'right away' and 'death or serious harm'.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Medical emergency: Sudden, Serious, Right away.
Memory tip 2: Multidisciplinary: many disciplines, one goal.
Memory tip 3: Trauma: two types, blunt and penetrating.

questions.text: Differentiate between blunt and penetrating trauma, and define three (3) types of blunt injury.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Wound types appeared in the MCQs (avulsion, laceration, abrasion) in September 2022

askedIn.wording: Differentiate between blunt and penetrating trauma, and define three (3) types of blunt injury.

modelAnswer.intro: Trauma is classified by how the force reaches the body. The type of trauma decides the likely injuries and the way the nurse examines the patient.

subsections.heading: A. Five points to write
points: 1. Blunt trauma: the victim hits, or is hit by, a hard object; the skin may remain intact.
2. Penetrating (sharp force) trauma: the victim is poked, cut or stabbed, and an object pierces the skin, usually creating an open wound.
3. Contusion: blunt force ruptures the capillaries under intact skin (a bruise).
4. Abrasion: scraping off of the superficial epidermis.
5. Laceration: blunt force tears the skin.

subsections.heading: B. Extra points
points: 6. Penetrating wounds can hide serious internal injury, so the mechanism and pattern of injury are always documented.
7. Penetrating trauma to the chest or abdomen needs rapid assessment of airway, breathing and circulation.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Compare the two types on how the force acts and on the state of the skin, then define the three blunt injuries.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Types of Trauma section).

questions.text: Describe the trimodal distribution of trauma deaths, stating the timing and one cause for each peak.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Very High · The trimodal distribution was an MCQ in 3 of 5 papers and has never been set as an SAQ

askedIn.wording: Describe the trimodal distribution of trauma deaths, stating the timing and one cause for each peak.

modelAnswer.intro: The trimodal distribution describes the three peaks in time at which patients die after serious injury. It explains why rapid, organised trauma care saves lives.

subsections.heading: A. Three peaks to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. First peak, within seconds to minutes: lacerations of the heart, great vessels, brain or spinal cord. These deaths can only be prevented by injury prevention.
2. Second peak, within minutes to hours: intracranial haematomas and uncontrolled haemorrhage (for example pelvic fractures, solid organ lacerations and multiple wounds).
3. Third peak, within days to weeks: sepsis, multi-organ failure, and respiratory and other complications.

subsections.heading: B. Why this matters
points: 4. The second peak is the one that the emergency nurse can change, through rapid assessment and control of bleeding.
5. The third peak is reduced by good critical care and infection control.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Give the timing and the cause of each peak in order: first, second, third.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Trimodal Distribution section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: the MCQs ask 'the second peak is due to...' and put sepsis and multi-organ failure as options. Those belong to the THIRD peak.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Seconds, Hours, Weeks: Sudden, Slow bleed, Sepsis. First = sudden destruction, second = bleeding or brain clot, third = sepsis and organ failure.
Memory tip 2: Intracranial haematoma and haemorrhage are the second peak; sepsis and multi-organ failure are the third.
Memory tip 3: Past MCQs: April 2024 and April 2025 asked about the second peak (answer: intracranial haematoma) and September 2024 asked about the third peak (answer: sepsis).

questions.text: Outline four (4) steps the emergency nurse takes to ensure scene safety before giving care.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Safety was an MCQ in September 2022 and September 2024; the steps have not been set as an SAQ

askedIn.wording: Outline four (4) steps the emergency nurse takes to ensure scene safety before giving care.

modelAnswer.intro: Scene safety means assessing and managing the environment to identify hazards before giving care. It protects the nurse, other responders and bystanders. The first rule is: do not risk your life.

subsections.heading: A. Four steps to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Determine the number of patients.
2. Determine the equipment needed for extrication: cervical collar, bandages, PPE, long backboard and straps, and a rigid extrication collar.
3. Have oxygen and airway equipment ready, including suction and a bag-valve mask (BVM).
4. Have a trauma box or bag: bandages, haemostatic agent, tourniquet, BP cuff and stethoscope.

subsections.heading: B. Other safety points
points: 5. Look for hazards such as falling or burning structures, hostile crowds and shooting, and stay off roadways.
6. Wear PPE and use barrier devices.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write the four steps in the order given in the notes and add the key equipment in brackets.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Scene Safety section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not confuse scene safety with standard precautions. Scene safety looks at the environment; standard precautions protect against infection (next question).

Memory tip 2: A hurt rescuer helps nobody, so the safety of the responder is a priority aspect (tested in the September 2022 MCQ); the notes say 'do not risk your life'.
Memory tip 3: The September 2024 MCQ listed unsafe situations (hostile crowd, unstable building, shoot-outs) and the safe one (switching off the car engine).

2. Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette.

parts.title: Shock: Pathophysiology and Types
parts.frequencyBadge: Predicted: High · Shock appears in the MCQs in every paper

questions.text: Define shock and outline the cellular pathophysiology of shock.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Shock is in the MCQs in every paper and the definition has not been tested yet

askedIn.wording: Define shock and outline the cellular pathophysiology of shock.

modelAnswer.intro: Shock is a clinical syndrome that results from inadequate tissue perfusion, creating an imbalance between oxygen and nutrient delivery and the needs of the cells. Normal perfusion needs four intact components: the vessels, an adequate intravascular volume, adequate gas exchange in the lungs and a functioning pump (the heart).

subsections.heading: A. Four points to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Definition: a clinical syndrome from inadequate tissue perfusion, with an imbalance between oxygen and nutrient delivery and cellular needs.
2. Without oxygen, cells switch from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism. The ATP yield is low and lactic acid accumulates.
3. The intracellular environment becomes acidotic. Mitochondria are damaged, cells swell, membranes become permeable and electrolytes and fluid shift.
4. Cells die across many organs. This is the systemic inflammatory response (SIRS), which leads to multi-organ failure and death.

subsections.heading: B. Related points
points: 5. The four components of normal perfusion: the vascular system, intravascular volume, lung gas exchange and a functioning heart.
6. Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume (about 5 L/min at rest; stroke volume about 70 mL).

modelAnswer.conclusion: State the definition first and then follow the three steps of the cell story in order.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Shock Pathophysiology section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not write the signs or management of shock; this question is about what happens to the cell.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: No oxygen, so anaerobic; anaerobic, so lactic acid; acid, so swollen leaky cells; leaky cells die, so organs fail.
Memory tip 2: ALD: Anaerobic, Lactic acidosis with cell swelling, Death of cells (SIRS and multi-organ failure).

questions.text: State five (5) late signs of hypovolaemic shock.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Early versus late signs were tested in the MCQs in April 2024 and September 2024

askedIn.wording: State five (5) late signs of hypovolaemic shock.

modelAnswer.intro: Late (decompensated) shock occurs when the body can no longer compensate for the loss of volume. Late signs mean that the patient is close to death and needs immediate resuscitation.

subsections.heading: A. Five late signs to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Unresponsiveness with dilated pupils.
2. Central cyanosis and respiratory failure.
3. Cool, clammy, mottled, grey skin with absent peripheral pulses.
4. Hypotension and bradycardia, with anuria.
5. Lactate above 4 mmol/L and a base deficit worse than minus 4.

subsections.heading: B. Other late signs
points: 6. Absent bowel sounds.
7. Electrolyte imbalance, DIC (bleeding from multiple sites) and thrombocytopenia.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Choose signs from different systems.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Hypovolaemic Shock section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: tachycardia, anxiety, pallor and reduced urine output are EARLY signs. Anuria (no urine) and bradycardia are LATE.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Early is fast and restless; late is slow and silent.
Memory tip 2: Hypotension appears late in shock because the body holds the pressure up until it fails.
Memory tip 3: Lactate: above 2 is early, above 4 is late.
