questions.text: Outline five (5) nursing interventions in the management of cardiogenic shock.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Causes of cardiogenic shock were tested in April 2025 and the type in September 2024

askedIn.wording: Outline five (5) nursing interventions in the management of cardiogenic shock.

modelAnswer.intro: In cardiogenic shock the heart fails as a pump (for example after a myocardial infarction), so the aim of treatment is to improve oxygenation and reduce the work of the heart.

subsections.heading: A. Five interventions to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Secure the airway and give high-flow oxygen; intubate and ventilate if needed.
2. Position the patient in semi-Fowler's or Fowler's position to reduce the cardiac workload.
3. Reduce preload with vasodilators or diuretics.
4. Give morphine for pain relief and vasodilation, and nitroglycerin for vasodilation.
5. Give dobutamine to improve contractility.

subsections.heading: B. Causes (for reference)
points: 6. Myocardial infarction, ventricular ischaemia, dysrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, valve disease, chest trauma and drugs such as beta-blockers and antihypertensives.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Remember that the problem is the pump, not the volume.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Cardiogenic Shock section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not give a large fluid bolus as in hypovolaemic shock. The notes use diuretics to reduce volume.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Hypovolaemic is thirsty, so give fluid. Cardiogenic is waterlogged, so reduce fluid.
Memory tip 2: Oxygen, Position, Dilate the vessels, Morphine and Nitroglycerin, and Dobutamine to make the heart squeeze harder.
Memory tip 3: Diuretics reduce intravascular volume, which reduces the work of the heart.

questions.text: Outline neurogenic shock, stating its commonest cause, two (2) signs and two (2) management measures.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · Neurogenic shock is the distributive type linked to spinal injury in the notes

askedIn.wording: Outline neurogenic shock, stating its commonest cause, two (2) signs and two (2) management measures.

modelAnswer.intro: Neurogenic shock is a type of distributive shock caused by loss of sympathetic tone, which leads to widespread vasodilation.

subsections.heading: A. Five points to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Commonest cause: spinal cord injury (others are deep general or spinal anaesthesia, brain damage and toxins).
2. Sign: bradycardia with hypotension (SBP below 90 or 30 below baseline).
3. Sign: warm, dry, flushed skin with temperature dysregulation.
4. Management: ABCs first, to prevent secondary cord injury.
5. Management: vasopressors (norepinephrine or epinephrine infusion) and atropine for bradycardia.

subsections.heading: B. Contrast
points: 6. Unlike hypovolaemic shock, the skin is warm and dry and the heart rate is slow.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Give the cause, the two signs and the two measures.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Neurogenic Shock section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: bradycardia and warm dry skin are what make neurogenic shock different from other types of shock, which have tachycardia and cool clammy skin.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Neurogenic means the nerves have lost control of the vessels: slow heart, low pressure, warm dry skin.
Memory tip 2: Think spinal injury plus bradycardia: neurogenic shock.

modelAnswer.intro: Septic shock is the most common distributive shock and the last, most severe stage of sepsis. The gram-negative bacteria are the commonest cause.

subsections.heading: A. Five measures to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Treat the cause with antibiotics (gram-negatives are the most common).
2. Give IV crystalloids or colloids.
3. Give oxygen; the patient is often mechanically ventilated.
4. Give low-dose corticosteroids (hydrocortisone) for adrenal insufficiency, and insulin to control sepsis-related hyperglycaemia.
5. Give nutrition within 24 to 48 hours.

subsections.heading: B. Other points
points: 6. Anticoagulants (heparin) limit unneeded clotting.
7. Predisposing factors: malnutrition, immunosuppression, invasive procedures, age over 80, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, burns and substance abuse.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Start with the cause, which is the infection.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Septic Shock section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not write the management of anaphylactic shock (epinephrine) or neurogenic shock (vasopressors and atropine).

Memory tip 2: Hydrocortisone is for adrenal insufficiency; insulin is for the high sugar.

questions.text: Differentiate between a superficial partial-thickness burn and a full-thickness burn.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · Burn depth was an MCQ in April 2025 and has never been set as an SAQ

askedIn.wording: Differentiate between a superficial partial-thickness burn and a full-thickness burn.

modelAnswer.intro: Burns are classified by depth according to the layers of skin that are damaged. Depth decides the appearance, the pain, the healing time and the need for grafting.

subsections.heading: A. Four points to write (2 marks for each burn)
points: 1. Superficial partial-thickness burn: involves the epidermis and part of the dermis; the skin is wet, shiny and weeping with blisters, painful, and it blanches (appendages are intact).
2. It heals in about 2 weeks with minimal scarring.

3. Full-thickness burn: involves the entire dermis and possibly fat, muscle and bone; the skin is pale white, brown or charred and leathery, painless, does not blanch, and the vessels are thrombosed (follicles and glands are destroyed).
4. It needs grafting or amputation and leaves scarring and contractures.

subsections.heading: B. Other depths from the notes
points: 5. Superficial (first degree), for example sunburn: epidermis only, red, dry and painful, no blisters; it peels in 3 to 7 days without scarring.
6. Deep partial-thickness: blisters that open easily, oedema, no blanching; it heals in 2 to 4 weeks with scarring and contractures and may convert to full thickness if infected.
7. Severity can be deceiving, because full-thickness burns are painless.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Use two columns or two short paragraphs, one for each burn, and compare layers, appearance, pain and healing.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Burn Depth section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: the full-thickness burn is PAINLESS because the nerve endings are destroyed. A burn that is white, leathery and painless (as in the April 2025 MCQ) is full thickness.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Wet and weeping with pain is superficial partial thickness; dry, leathery and painless is full thickness.
Memory tip 2: Painful means nerves alive; painless means nerves destroyed.
Memory tip 3: Healing time rises with depth: 3 to 7 days, about 2 weeks, 2 to 4 weeks, then grafting.

questions.text: Describe three (3) methods of estimating the extent of a burn (percentage of total body surface area).
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · The Rule of Nines is needed for every Parkland calculation

askedIn.wording: Describe three (3) methods of estimating the extent of a burn (percentage of total body surface area).

modelAnswer.intro: The extent of a burn is expressed as the percentage of the total body surface area (TBSA) that is burned. The estimate is made on arrival and revised within 72 hours, when the depth becomes clearer.

subsections.heading: A. Four points to write
points: 1. Rule of Nines (adults): head and neck 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18% and genitalia 1%.

2. Lund and Browder chart: the gold standard and the best for children, because it uses age-specific percentages (a child's head is relatively larger and the legs smaller; the head is 19% at 0 to 1 year, 17% at 1 to 4, 13% at 5 to 9, 11% at 10 to 14, 9% at 15 and 7% in adults).
3. Palmar method: the patient's palm with fingers is about 1% TBSA (the palm alone about 0.5%); it is used for scattered or small burns and quick prehospital estimates.
4. The estimate is made on arrival and revised within 72 hours.

subsections.heading: B. Cautions
points: 5. The palmar method may over- or underestimate, for example in obesity.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Name each method, say who it is for and give one figure.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Burn Extent section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not use the Rule of Nines for children. The head of a child is a larger proportion of the body than that of an adult.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Nines: 9, 9, 18, 18, 18, 1 add up to 100.
Memory tip 2: Children need Lund and Browder because the head is big and the legs are small.
Memory tip 3: A palm is about 1% of the body surface.

questions.text: State five (5) systemic responses to a major burn (more than 20% TBSA).
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · The systemic response is the longest part of the burn pathophysiology in the notes

askedIn.wording: State five (5) systemic responses to a major burn (more than 20% TBSA).

modelAnswer.intro: A burn of more than 20% TBSA is a major burn and causes a response in the whole body, not just in the skin.

subsections.heading: A. Five responses to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Cardiovascular: rapid plasma loss reduces cardiac output and blood pressure, which is the onset of burn shock; catecholamines cause vasoconstriction and tachycardia, and haemoconcentration increases the risk of thrombosis.
2. Electrolytes: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis.
3. Gastrointestinal: paralytic ileus and Curling's ulcer.
4. Renal: hypovolaemia and free haemoglobin and myoglobin block the tubules and can cause acute tubular necrosis and renal failure.
5. Thermoregulation: loss of skin causes heat loss and hypothermia.

subsections.heading: B. Other systemic points
points: 6. Pulmonary: inhalation injury causes airway oedema and hypoxaemia.
7. Fluid shifts: the maximum leak is in the first 24 to 36 hours, peaking at 6 to 8 hours; remobilisation follows at about 24 to 48 hours, and red cell destruction may cause anaemia.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Name the system and one effect for each point.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Burns: Systemic Response section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: the LOCAL response (oedema, evaporation, haematocrit) is for burns of 20% or less and is a separate answer.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Systems: Heart, Salts, Gut, Kidney, Temperature (and lungs).
Memory tip 2: Sodium is lost into the tissue (hyponatraemia), but potassium is released from cells (hyperkalaemia).

questions.text: Outline the three (3) phases of burn management.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · The phase is the key to every 'emergent phase' or 'acute phase' question

askedIn.wording: Outline the three (3) phases of burn management.

modelAnswer.intro: Burn management is divided into three phases. Knowing the phase tells the nurse which interventions belong in the answer.

subsections.heading: A. Three phases to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Emergent (resuscitative) phase: from the time of injury to the completion of fluid resuscitation (24 to 48 hours).
2. Acute (intermediate) phase: from the start of diuresis to near wound closure (48 hours to weeks).
3. Rehabilitation phase: from wound closure to optimal physical and psychosocial adjustment.

subsections.heading: B. Focus of each phase
points: 4. Emergent: first aid, fluid resuscitation, preventing respiratory distress and pain control.
5. Acute: infection prevention, wound care, nutrition and preventing contractures.
6. Rehabilitation: pressure garments, scar management and psychosocial recovery.

questions.text: Outline five (5) nursing interventions in the acute phase of burn management.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · The emergent phase was asked in 2025, so the acute phase is the natural next question

askedIn.wording: Outline five (5) nursing interventions in the acute phase of burn management.

modelAnswer.intro: In the acute phase, which starts at about 48 to 72 hours, the aims are to keep up support, prevent infection and help the wound to heal.

subsections.heading: A. Five interventions to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Prevent infection: use PPE and aseptic technique, apply topical antibacterials and isolate the patient in a positive-pressure room.
2. Wound care: debridement, hydrotherapy, grafting, escharotomy, and dressings that keep the wound warm and moist.
3. Prevent contractures with daily exercise and splinting, and elevate burned upper limbs above the heart to reduce oedema.
4. Give nutrition: enteral feeding within 24 to 48 hours to prevent ileus, and parenteral nutrition if enteral feeding is not tolerated.
5. Continue pain and anxiety management, and give tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics for contaminated wounds.

subsections.heading: B. Other interventions
points: 6. Continue respiratory, circulatory, fluid, electrolyte and gastrointestinal support.
7. Check weight daily to avoid fluid overload, and take photographs to document the burn.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write only acute phase actions.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Burns: Acute Phase section).

Memory tip 2: Positive-pressure room keeps germs out; the patient is the one who needs protecting.

questions.text: State four (4) topical antibacterial agents used in burn care and one important nursing consideration for each.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · The agent table is the largest table in the burn notes

askedIn.wording: State four (4) topical antibacterial agents used in burn care and one important nursing consideration for each.

modelAnswer.intro: Topical antibacterial agents are applied to the burn wound in the acute phase to prevent infection. Each agent has its own precautions.

subsections.heading: A. Four agents to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Silver sulfadiazine 1%: most bactericidal, minimal eschar penetration; watch for leukopenia (2 to 3 days) and pseudo-eschar.

2. Mafenide acetate 5 to 10%: penetrates eschar and is the agent of choice for electrical burns; it causes severe pain (premedicate) and is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, so monitor for metabolic acidosis.
3. Silver nitrate 0.5%: bacteriostatic and fungicidal, does not penetrate eschar; keep the dressing wet, monitor sodium and potassium (hypotonic), and note that it stains black.
4. Acticoat: silver-impregnated dressing; moisten with sterile water only (never saline); it can stay on for 3 to 5 days (Acticoat 7: up to 7 days) and no oil-based products are used.

subsections.heading: B. Extra
points: 5. Silver sulfadiazine is applied as a 1/16-inch layer 1 to 3 times a day.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Give the agent and one consideration.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Topical Antibacterials section).

askedIn.wording: State five (5) complications of burns.

modelAnswer.intro: Burn complications can affect the skin, the gut, the blood, the nerves and the mind. Some are prevented by good nursing care.

subsections.heading: A. Five complications to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Contractures (prevented by positioning and exercise).
2. Curling's ulcer.
3. Paralytic ileus.
4. Sepsis.
5. Hypertrophic and keloid scars.

subsections.heading: B. Other complications
points: 6. Emotional damage, anaemia, peripheral neuropathies and amputation.
7. Eschar or compartment syndrome: a deep circumferential burn forms inelastic eschar that acts like a tourniquet and is relieved by an escharotomy (a surgical incision into the eschar).

modelAnswer.conclusion: State each complication in one line.

questions.text: Outline the adult basic life support (BLS) sequence from scene safety to rescue breaths.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · BLS sequence steps appeared in the MCQs in 3 of 5 papers

askedIn.wording: Outline the adult basic life support (BLS) sequence from scene safety to rescue breaths.

modelAnswer.intro: The adult BLS sequence is: Safety, Stimulate, Shout, Check pulse and breathing, Airway, Breathing. It is followed whenever a collapsed person is found.

subsections.heading: A. Six steps to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Safety: check the scene, yourself and the victim; wear PPE and use barrier devices; do not risk your life.
2. Stimulate: tap and shout 'are you OK?' on both sides and tap or shake the shoulders.
3. Shout for help: state the location and ask for an AED and a BVM, or call emergency services.
4. Check pulse and breathing: carotid pulse and chest rise for 5 to 10 seconds. If there is no pulse, start CPR; if there is a pulse but no normal breathing, give 1 breath every 6 seconds.
5. Airway: head-tilt chin-lift, or jaw thrust if head or neck injury is suspected.
6. Breathing: give 2 breaths, each over 1 second with visible chest rise, by mouth-to-mask, bag-valve mask or mouth-to-mouth.

subsections.heading: B. After the sequence
points: 7. If breathing and pulse are present, monitor until help arrives and use the recovery position if unconscious.
8. High-quality CPR then follows (30:2, 100 to 120 per minute, at least 5 cm).

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write the six steps in order with one detail each.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Adult BLS Sequence section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: the sequence is for finding and starting; high-quality CPR is a separate question (Q13). Gasping is not effective breathing.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Safety, Stimulate, Shout, Check, Airway, Breathing: 4 S-words then A and B.
Memory tip 2: The 2025 MCQ: after an unresponsive finding, the next step is to shout for help.
Memory tip 3: Check the pulse for no more than 10 seconds.

questions.text: Define the following terms: (a) cardiac arrest, (b) respiratory arrest, (c) cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), (d) automated external defibrillator (AED).
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · BLS definitions are the first block of the BLS notes

askedIn.wording: Define the following terms: (a) cardiac arrest, (b) respiratory arrest, (c) cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), (d) automated external defibrillator (AED).

modelAnswer.intro: These definitions are short and exact, so learn the wording of the notes.

subsections.heading: A. Four definitions to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Cardiac arrest: cessation of the heartbeat.
2. Respiratory arrest: cessation of breathing, leading to cardiac arrest within minutes. Gasping is not effective breathing.
3. CPR: external maintenance of circulation and respiration through chest compressions and artificial ventilation.
4. AED: a portable computerised device that identifies shockable rhythms and delivers a shock to restore a normal rhythm.

subsections.heading: B. Related definition and goals
points: 5. BLS: rapid interventions by health workers or laypeople to recognise sudden cardiac arrest and collapse due to foreign body airway obstruction, heart attack or stroke.
6. Goals of BLS: restore cardiorespiratory function, maintain brain viability, optimise survival and prevent cardiac arrest.

modelAnswer.conclusion: One sentence per term.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (BLS Definitions section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not define CPR as only chest compressions; it also includes artificial ventilation.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Cardiac arrest = heart stops. Respiratory arrest = breathing stops, heart stops soon after.
Memory tip 2: AED = a machine that finds a shockable rhythm and shocks it.

questions.text: Describe how to give rescue breaths using a bag-valve mask (BVM), and what to do if the chest does not rise.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · The BVM technique is detailed in the notes

askedIn.wording: Describe how to give rescue breaths using a bag-valve mask (BVM), and what to do if the chest does not rise.

modelAnswer.intro: The bag-valve mask is the preferred way to give rescue breaths in a healthcare setting. Each breath must give a visible chest rise.

subsections.heading: A. Five points to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Use a transparent mask with a good seal over the nose and mouth.
2. Use a C-E clamp grip to hold the mask.
3. Attach an oxygen reservoir.
4. Give each breath over 1 second with visible chest rise (2 breaths after 30 compressions).
5. If the chest does not rise: reposition the head, adjust the fingers and seal, check for obstruction and consider an airway adjunct.

subsections.heading: B. Other methods and airway opening
points: 6. Other methods are mouth-to-mask and mouth-to-mouth.
7. Open the airway with head-tilt chin-lift, or jaw thrust if neck injury is suspected (use head-tilt chin-lift if the jaw thrust fails).

modelAnswer.conclusion: State the technique and the troubleshooting.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Rescue Breaths section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: a good seal and a visible chest rise are the two keywords.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: C-E clamp: C is the thumb and index finger on the mask, E is the other three fingers lifting the jaw.
Memory tip 2: No rise? Head, seal, obstruction, adjunct: H-S-O-A.

questions.text: Outline five (5) points in the technique of cardiopulmonary resuscitation in an infant.
questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: High · The infant ratio (15:2 with two rescuers) was an MCQ in April 2025

askedIn.wording: Outline five (5) points in the technique of cardiopulmonary resuscitation in an infant.

modelAnswer.intro: Infancy ends at 1 year. Cardiac arrest in children is commonly due to respiratory arrest.

subsections.heading: A. Five points to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Place the infant on a firm surface and check the brachial pulse (carotid in a child) for up to 10 seconds.
2. Compress the lower sternum just below the nipple line, with two fingers or the heel of one hand, or with the two-thumb encircling-hands technique.
3. Compress to a depth of one-third of the chest (about 4 cm) at 100 to 120 per minute, with full recoil.
4. Use a ratio of 30:2 for a single rescuer and 15:2 with two rescuers.
5. A healthcare professional first gives 5 rescue breaths if the infant is not breathing normally; reassess after every 5 cycles.

subsections.heading: B. Child differences
points: 6. In a child, use the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum, avoiding the xiphoid.
7. An off-duty rescuer finding an unresponsive child gives BLS for about 2 minutes and then calls EMS.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write the site, the depth, the rate and the ratio.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Infant CPR section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: adult depth is at least 5 cm; infant depth is one-third of the chest. The two-rescuer ratio for infants and children is 15:2, not 30:2.
memoryTips: Memory tip 1: Infant: lower sternum below the nipple line, one-third depth, 15:2 with two rescuers.
Memory tip 2: Adult 30:2 always; child and infant 15:2 only with two rescuers.

questions.text: State four (4) signs of severe airway obstruction in a child and name two (2) infections that can cause airway obstruction.

askedIn.wording: State four (4) signs of severe airway obstruction in a child and name two (2) infections that can cause airway obstruction.

modelAnswer.intro: Airway obstruction in children is caused by croup (a viral infection below the vocal cords), epiglottitis (an infection above the cords) or a foreign body.

subsections.heading: A. Five points to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Ineffective (silent) cough.
2. Inability to cry or speak.
3. Increasing difficulty with stridor.
4. Cyanosis or loss of consciousness.
5. Infections that cause airway obstruction: croup and epiglottitis.

subsections.heading: B. General signs of airway obstruction
points: 6. Reduced or absent breath sounds, stridor, retractions and difficulty speaking.
7. If the cough is effective, encourage coughing and monitor for deterioration.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Write the four signs and the two infections.

modelAnswer.intro: Cardiac arrest in children is commonly due to respiratory arrest, so the first priority is the airway and breathing.

4. Call the resuscitation team after 1 minute, then continue CPR.

questions.frequencyText: Predicted probability: Medium-High · Seizure first aid was set in April 2025; causes and hospital care have not been

askedIn.wording: State five (5) causes of seizures and outline the hospital care of a patient who has continuous convulsions.

modelAnswer.intro: A seizure is an episode of abnormal motor, sensory, autonomic or psychic activity caused by a sudden excessive neuronal discharge.

subsections.heading: A. Five points to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Causes: idiopathic or genetic, cerebrovascular disease and hypoxaemia.
2. Causes: childhood fever and head injury.
3. Causes: hypertension, brain tumour, drug or alcohol withdrawal and allergies.
4. Hospital care: suction if needed, give oxygen and place the bed low with padded side rails.
5. Give IV diazepam 10 mg only if convulsions are continuous or recur.

subsections.heading: B. Remember
points: 6. First aid is about safety and airway; drugs belong to hospital care.

modelAnswer.conclusion: Group the causes into two or three lines.
modelAnswer.contentSupport: Trauma, Emergency Nursing and First Aid consolidated summary (lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri, MSN, drawing on Sheehy's Emergency Nursing Principles and Practice, 7th ed., and AHA material) (Seizures section).

questions.warningNotice: Exam trap: do not write first aid steps (stay with the person, cushion the head) when the question asks for hospital care.

modelAnswer.intro: Spinal injury can lead to paralysis. Moving the patient wrongly can worsen it.

subsections.heading: A. Five points to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Signs: awkward body position.

4. First aid: keep the head in line with the neck and avoid twisting.
5. Support the neck with a rolled cloth or towel and do not move the patient unless there is an urgent need.

modelAnswer.intro: Antivenin neutralises venom but must be used carefully.

subsections.heading: A. Four points to write (1 mark each)
points: 1. Monitor the patient for at least 6 hours to decide on antivenin.
2. Antivenin is not used for mild or resolving symptoms.
3. It is indicated for any progressive pain, swelling or ecchymosis.
4. It is made from animal serum and carries a risk of life-threatening allergic reactions.

points: 5. Send coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer) and give tetanus prophylaxis.

modelAnswer.intro: Stroke is ischaemic (85%) or haemorrhagic (15%).

points: 6. Signs: sudden numbness or weakness of the face, arm or leg, severe headache, dizziness, visual disturbance, confusion.
